III. Quoad Articulum de Persona Christi, convenit inter utrosque (pag. 13. 14. 15. 16.): 1. Divinam et Humanam Naturam revera et personaliter esse unitas, sic ut Christus Deus et Homo sit, in Personae unitate; et illam Unionem factam esse ἀσυγχύτως, ἀτρέπτως, ἀδιαιρέτως, ἀχωρίστως — inconfuse, citra mutationem, indivisim, et inseparabiliter. 2. Nomina Naturarum de se invicem vere, et in propria verborum significatione praedicari: Deus est Homo, Homo est Deus; Proprietates etiam utriusque Naturae unitae, de tota Persona in concreto vere et realiter praedicari, sed secundum illam Naturam, cui istae Proprietates vel Attributa re vera conveniunt — quam Communicationem Idiomatum Theologis appellare placuit. 3. Naturam Humanam non esse intrinsece omnipotentem, nec omnisciam; sic in Unione, Naturas unitas mansisse distinctas, et Proprietates utriusque essentiales salvas; Principium quod agit esse Personam, Principium quo, Naturam utramque, etc. 4. Humanam Naturam vere ad summam gloriam evectam esse, sedentem quoque et ipsam ad Dextram Dei. 5. Rejici utrimque Nestorii, Eutychis, Marcionis, Arii, Photini, Pauli Samosateni, Socini (hoc ordine locant) ac similium Haereses.

Remansit dissensus, nec is essentialis a Viris illis agnitus: 1. An Naturae Humanae in abstracto communicata esset Majestas divina, seu Omnis potestas, quam exerceret per Omnipotentiam ubique praesentem, ac sibi hypostatice conjunctam? 2. An de eadem Natura Humana, in abstracto, praedicari possent Proprietates divinae, quae ad operandum sunt comparatae, Omnipotentia, etc.

IV. Quoad Articulum de S. Baptismo, utrimque in istud consenserunt (pag. 17. 18.): Quod Infantes sint baptizandi; quod Baptismi finis sit, ut Christo inferantur, et spiritualiter regenerentur; quod Baptismus necessarius sit, nec tamen absolute, ita ut solus contemptus Baptismi damnet; quod Infantes sint capaces gratiae regenerantis: atque haec ad essentialia ejus Sacramenti pertinere Pars utraque statuit. Remanserunt Controversiae, utrimque tamen agnitae non essentiales: 1. An Infantes demum per Baptismum Christo inferantur et regenerentur, necessitate medii, ordinarii scilicet? 2. An propter periculum, ex neglectu Baptismi, in casu necessitatis, etiam Laicus Baptismum administrare possit, si negetur Ministri copia?

V. Ceremonias quod attinet, puta Exorcismum in formula Baptismi, consensum utrimque est: 1. Non existimandum, infantem a Satana corporaliter esse possessum. 2. Ritum illum non aliter adhiberi posse, quam ad significandam Peccati Originalis habitualem inhaerentiam. 3. Omitti posse Exorcismi illas formulas, et in expressas Preces commutari.

Atque ad hujus Consensionis normam, in eandem societatem censuerunt dicti Theologi invitandas esse Academias Ecclesiasque Germaniae, cumprimis (ut viciniores) Brandenburgicas et Brunsvicenses. Et huic laudatissimo studio totum incubuisse, ab annis compluribus, pro iis quibus succendebatur pietatis et charitatis ignibus, Germaniae illum Mavortem vere Christianum, Libertatis juxta et Religionis Statorem, FRIDERICUM WILHELMUM, S. R. I. Electorem, animo juxta et armis Invictissimum, ut testis est Europa, sic nos quoque et olim, et non diu ante fata, in tanti Principis Sacrarium et colloquium admissi.
english: III. As to the Article concerning the Person of Christ, both sides agreed (pp. 13–16): 1. That the Divine and Human Nature are truly and personally united, so that Christ is God and Man in the unity of Person; and that that Union was made ἀσυγχύτως, ἀτρέπτως, ἀδιαιρέτως, ἀχωρίστως — without confusion, without change, indivisibly, and inseparably. 2. That the Names of the Natures are truly predicated of each other, and in the proper signification of the words: God is Man, Man is God; and that the Properties also of each united Nature are truly and really predicated of the whole Person in the concrete, but according to that Nature to which those Properties or Attributes truly belong — which the Theologians have been pleased to call the Communication of Properties (Communicatio Idiomatum). 3. That the Human Nature is not intrinsically omnipotent, nor omniscient; thus in the Union the united Natures remained distinct, and the essential Properties of each safe; that the Principle which acts is the Person, the Principle by which, each Nature, and so on. 4. That the Human Nature has truly been raised to the highest glory, sitting also itself at the Right Hand of God. 5. That on both sides the Heresies of Nestorius, Eutyches, Marcion, Arius, Photinus, Paul of Samosata, Socinus (they place them in this order), and the like, are rejected.

There remained a dissent, and one not acknowledged as essential by those Men: 1. Whether to the Human Nature in the abstract there was communicated the divine Majesty, or All power, which it would exercise through the Omnipotence everywhere present and hypostatically joined to it? 2. Whether of the same Human Nature, in the abstract, there could be predicated the divine Properties that are fitted for operating — Omnipotence, and so on.

IV. As to the Article concerning Holy Baptism, both sides consented to this (pp. 17–18): That Infants are to be baptized; that the end of Baptism is that they be grafted into Christ and spiritually regenerated; that Baptism is necessary, yet not absolutely, so that only contempt of Baptism damns; that Infants are capable of regenerating grace: and both Parties established that these things belong to the essentials of that Sacrament. Controversies remained, yet acknowledged on both sides as not essential: 1. Whether Infants are at last grafted into Christ and regenerated through Baptism by the necessity of a means — namely an ordinary means? 2. Whether, because of the danger from neglect of Baptism, in a case of necessity, even a Layman may administer Baptism if a Minister's supply is denied?

V. As to Ceremonies — for example Exorcism in the Baptismal formula — there was consent on both sides: 1. That it is not to be thought the infant is corporally possessed by Satan. 2. That that rite can be employed no otherwise than to signify the habitual inherence of Original Sin. 3. That those formulas of Exorcism can be omitted and changed into express Prayers.

And according to the norm of this Agreement, the said Theologians judged that the Academies and Churches of Germany — especially (as nearer) the Brandenburg and Brunswick ones — ought to be invited into the same fellowship. And that truly Christian Mars of Germany, Assertor of Liberty as well as of Religion, FREDERICK WILLIAM, Elector of the Holy Roman Empire, most Invincible alike in mind and in arms — as Europe is witness, and as we too once were, and not long before his death, admitted into so great a Prince's sanctuary and conversation — had for many years wholly devoted himself to this most praiseworthy zeal, according to those fires of piety and charity with which he was kindled.

source_text:
Ibant quo poterant! Piorum certe quorumcunque Theologorum est, ministram operam adhibere, neque dictis tantum, aut scriptis, sed et factis; scilicet vera charitate accensis et cordibus, et linguis, et calamis, compositisque domesticis dissidiis, inter consortes ejusdem Fidei, atque Tesserae. Quod posterius, de universis aut plerisque, optandum magis est quam sperandum, donec erit humanis affectibus atque infirmitatibus locus.

Sint jam in Protestantium Virorum ordine, qui Errorem quemvis in Haeresin, aut Dissensum quemvis in Fundamentalem vel Essentialem, pro libidine vertant! Nihilominus persaepe verbalis ea dissensio fuerit, et circa phrasim vel enunciandi modum; ex. gr. in vocibus realiter, oraliter, sufficienter, efficaciter, &c. Saepe circa rei modum, puta rationem praesentiae vel adessentiae in Eucharistia. Aut circa rei circumstantias, puta Latitudinem Redemptionis — an et pro reprobis — manente re et substantia immotis. Saepe etiam dissensus non in vere traditis, sed in affictis, per consequentias non innatas, sed illatas, certe rejectas; v. gr. de negata a Reformatis Dei Omnipotentia, de Deo auctore Peccati, de Stoica necessitate asserta, &c. Denique dissidium privatum Theologorum magis, quam publicum Confessionum, in non una quaestione, Fratres distraxit: Qualiter in quaestione Supralapsaria, fere sopita, aliisque id genus quam plurimis.
english: They went as far as they could! It belongs to pious Theologians of every sort to lend a helping hand — not by words or writings only, but also by deeds; that is, with hearts and tongues and pens kindled by true charity, and with domestic discords composed among the partners of the same Faith and of the same Token. That latter point, as concerns all or most, is more to be wished than hoped for, so long as there is still room for human affections and infirmities.

There are already in the rank of Protestant Men those who turn any Error into Heresy, or any Dissent into something Fundamental or Essential, as their passion wills! Nevertheless that dissent has very often been merely verbal, and has turned on phrasing or on the manner of stating a thing — for example in the words realiter, oraliter, sufficienter, efficaciter, and so on. Often it has turned on the mode of the thing — for instance the manner of presence or of being-present in the Eucharist. Or on the circumstances of the thing — for instance the Breadth of Redemption, whether also for the reprobate, while the thing itself and its substance remain unmoved. Often too the dissent is not in what was truly handed down, but in things fastened on by consequences not born in the teaching but brought in from outside — and certainly rejected; for example, that the Reformed deny God's Omnipotence, that they make God the author of Sin, that they assert a Stoic necessity, and so on. Finally, the private quarrel of Theologians more than the public quarrel of Confessions has pulled Brethren apart in more than one question: as in the Supralapsarian question, now nearly laid to sleep, and in very many others of that kind.

source_text: Addam et in illa de Potestate Majestatis circa Sacra, ab his magis restricta, ab aliis in Architectonicam versa: Vel etiam de limitibus Regiae Potestatis, et passivae obedientiae; Quo in argumento Theologus Hafniensis nuperus toti Reformatorum Ecclesiae, ex nonnullorum forte dictis vel assertis, in sensum quemcunque voluit, inflexis, hanc notam inussit parum verecunde, esse illam adversam et infestam Regum ac Principum juribus, vel etiam divinae istorum origini, imo et securitati: Nec alio instituto, quam ut Exules Gallos, in gremium Potentissimi Regis profugos, si non tecto, certe Templo, et libertate Sacrorum prohiberet. Procul a mea tuus sit furor omnis Domo! Ita sint nonnunquam Viri fratres, qui dicta saepe in disputationis aestu, saepe titubanter vel opinative, saepe sensu commodo, sed locutione incommoda, qualia primaevae Ecclesiae Scriptoribus et Patribus innumera exciderunt, parum Christiane in contentionis argumentum et λογομαχιῶν, avidissime rapiant! Sint qui in cogitatis quibusdam suis, aut sensu suo abundent, in praejudicium Ecclesiasticae tranquillitatis, et contra prudentiae Christianae leges! Sint qui privatorum naevos in publicos Ecclesiarum transformant: sic dicta quaedam, v. gr. Zwinglii, Calvini, Martyris, Bezae, &c. in sententiam Eccl. Reformatae, et duriore quidem sensu intellecta!
english: I will add also that dispute concerning the Power of Majesty about Sacred things — more restricted by some, turned by others into an Architectonic power; or even concerning the limits of Royal Power and of passive obedience. On that argument a recent Theologian of Copenhagen has, with little modesty, branded the whole Reformed Church — twisting certain sayings or assertions of a few into whatever sense he wished — as adverse and hostile to the rights of Kings and Princes, and even to their divine origin, and indeed to their security: and with no other design than that he might shut out the French Exiles, fled into the bosom of the Most Powerful King, if not from a roof, at least from the Temple and from the liberty of Sacred things. Far be all your fury from my House! So there are sometimes brother Men who, with little Christian spirit, most eagerly snatch sayings — often spoken in the heat of disputation, often hesitatingly or as opinion, often sound in sense but awkward in wording, such as fell in countless numbers from the Writers and Fathers of the early Church — into matter for contention and for battles about words (λογομαχίαι)! There are those who abound in certain private thoughts of their own, or in their own sense, to the prejudice of Ecclesiastical tranquillity and against the laws of Christian prudence! There are those who transform the blemishes of private men into public marks of the Churches: thus taking certain sayings, for example of Zwingli, Calvin, Martyr, Beza, and others, as the judgment of the Reformed Church, and understood in a harsher sense!

source_text:
Sint qui ex se ἀδιάφορα in necessaria, aut quae ad rationem externae disciplinae, vel ordinis, variam utique pro varietate Locorum, Gentium, Consuetudinum, in ipsam Christianismi substantiam, et quasi animam, abire jubeant! Sint qui fundamentalis quidem erroris (ut ἐπιεικῶς judicare prompti sumus) theoretice immunes, practico semet et graviori longe distinguant, charitatis nempe defectu, Matth. v. 23. 24. 1 Cor. xiii. 1. &c.! Certum jam fieri ista omnia, posthabito Servatoris nostri mandato, exemplo, charactere, ultimis verbis, Joh. xiv. 27. ac spretis divi Gentium Apostoli regulis monitisque Eph. iv. 2. 3. Phil. iii. 16. 1 Tim. vi. 4. &c. Neglecto etiam Ordinis sui decore et Officii; susque deque habitis sive piis Maximorum Principum studiis, sive ardentissimis Theologorum Partis utriusque votis, sive Bonorum omnium gemitibus ac suspiriis, nec attento Pacis Evangelicae instaurandae momento.

Nos sane haud intermittimus, seu lugere animo atque indolescere iniquissimis hominum affectibus, tanto cum veritatis Evangelicae dispendio, Ecclesiae damno, Hostium gaudio, Piorum offendiculo, Antichristianae tyrannidis incremento; seu etiam cum iis jungere dextras, quibus de meliore luto finxit praecordia Divinum Numen, qui de nobis nostrisque Ecclesiis sentiunt aequius ac moderatius, ac fundamentalem consensum intelligunt. Quales sunt, Dei beneficio, hinc inde varii per Germaniam pene omnem, et Arcticum Orbem; cumprimis luctosissimis temporibus, oppressa jam a communi Hoste Ecclesia, et deinceps opprimenda, nisi conjunctis et viribus et animis, sub auspiciis summarum Potestatum, furorem ista represserit. Jamque accipimus laetabundi, in amplissimis Ditionibus Potentissimi Brandenburgici, coalescere sensim studia, odia facessere, eristica arceri, in commune consuli, revocarique ad animos, ante concitatiores, quae hanc in rem suasere superiore et nostro Seculo Viri spectatae pietatis, moderationis prudentiaeque — Capitones, Buceri, Melanchthones, Strigelii, Peuceri, Pierii, Himmelii, Palladii, Donaweri, Chytraei, Pelargi, Osiandri, Calixti, Meyffarti, Matthiae, Dilheri, Drejeri, Conringii, Musaei, Heinichii, Helmstadienses, &c.
english: There are those who of themselves order things indifferent (ἀδιάφορα) to become necessary, or order what belongs to the pattern of external discipline or of order — variable of course with the variety of Places, Nations, and Customs — to pass over into the very substance of Christianity, and as it were its soul! There are those who, theoretically immune from fundamental error (as we are ready to judge gently, ἐπιεικῶς), yet distinguish themselves practically by something far heavier: namely by a defect of charity (Matthew 5:23-24; 1 Corinthians 13:1, and so on)! It is already certain that all these things are done when our Savior's mandate, example, character, and last words are set aside (John 14:27), and when the rules and warnings of the holy Apostle of the Gentiles are despised (Ephesians 4:2-3; Philippians 3:16; 1 Timothy 6:4, and so on). The dignity and Office of their own Order are neglected as well; the pious efforts of the Greatest Princes, the most ardent vows of Theologians of either Party, and the groans and sighs of all the Good are tossed up and down as of no account; and no attention is paid to the weight of restoring Evangelical Peace.

We for our part do not cease either to lament in spirit and to grow sick at heart over the most unjust affections of men — with so great a loss to Evangelical truth, harm to the Church, joy to Enemies, offense to the Pious, and increase of Antichristian tyranny — or also to join right hands with those for whom the Divine Majesty has shaped the heart of better clay, who think more fairly and moderately of us and of our Churches, and who understand the fundamental consensus. Such men there are, by God's kindness, here and there through nearly all Germany and the Northern world; especially in these most mournful times, when the Church is already oppressed by the common Enemy and will be oppressed still further unless, with forces and minds joined under the auspices of the highest Powers, she has repressed that fury. And already we hear with joy that in the ample Dominions of the Most Powerful Brandenburg Elector studies are gradually coalescing, hatreds are departing, eristic strife is being barred, common counsel is being taken, and there are being recalled to minds formerly more stirred what men of proven piety, moderation, and prudence urged in this matter in the last century and in ours — Capito, Bucer, Melanchthon, Strigelius, Peucer, Pierius, Himmel, Palladius, Donauer, Chytraeus, Pelargus, Osiander, Calixtus, Meyfart, Matthias, Dilher, Dreier, Conring, Musaeus, Heinich, the Helmstedt men, and others.

source_text: Atque utinam iretur ad primas dissensionum Origines, prolixe intellectas ex Historia Diffidii primum Sacramentarii, nati Anno 1524. inter Lutherum et Carolostadium, qui alias Bodenstein ex Carlstadt, mox Huldr. Zwinglio in mediam sententiam ituro: Scilicet Carolostadio, τὸ Hoc (τοῦτο) in verbis Institutionis referente non ad Panem, sed ad Corpus Christi, atque ita praesentiam omnem Corporis in Pane Eucharistico tollente; Luthero contra corporalem asserente, specie τοῦ ῥητοῦ; Zwinglio autem et Oecolampadio Sacramentalem, sub figura Panis et Vini. Intelligenda praecipue dissidiorum origine, ex illorum ingeniis qui horum certaminum pars magna fuere. Lutherus nempe fervidus, nec parem doctrina vel auctoritate satis ferens; Carolostadius minus prudens, impetu magis quam doctrina et judicio ductus; Zwinglius in sententia constans nec cedens Lutheri imperiis, vel nomini; Oecolampadius immotus, auctoritate Augustini, totiusque primae Antiquitatis; Melanchthon mitissimi ingenii, sic asserturus proprietatem Verborum institutionis, ut a Luthero discesserit, non agnita locali coexistentia, vel inclusione Corporis, nec hujus orali manducatione. Sed exceperunt mox Bellonae filii, acerba et eristica ingenia, lites auctura, et Controversias:
english: And would that men went back to the first Origins of the dissensions, understood at length from the History of the Diffidence — first the Sacramentarian schism, born in the year 1524 between Luther and Carolostadius, otherwise Bodenstein of Carlstadt, with Huldrych Zwingli soon about to move into a middle opinion: namely, Carolostadius referring the This (τοῦτο) in the words of Institution not to the Bread but to the Body of Christ, and so removing every presence of the Body in the Eucharistic Bread; Luther on the contrary asserting a corporal presence, by the letter of the text (τοῦ ῥητοῦ); but Zwingli and Oecolampadius a Sacramental presence, under the figure of Bread and Wine. The origin of the discords is to be understood especially from the temperaments of those who were a great part of these contests. Luther, to be sure, was fervid, and did not easily bear an equal in doctrine or authority; Carolostadius was less prudent, led by impulse more than by doctrine and judgment; Zwingli was constant in his opinion and yielded neither to Luther's commands nor to his name; Oecolampadius was unmoved, by the authority of Augustine and of the whole early Antiquity; Melanchthon, of the gentlest temper, would so assert the proper sense of the words of Institution that he departed from Luther, not acknowledging a local coexistence or inclusion of the Body, nor an oral manducation of it. But soon there came after them the sons of Bellona — bitter and eristic tempers — that would enlarge the suits and the Controversies:

source_text:
Quales Joh. Brentius Ubiquitariorum pater; Jac. Andrea, a fabrili arte Schmidlinus, superadditurus multa Brentianis; Tim. Heshusius tot turbarum fax flammarumque; Joh. Marbachius, novis portentis ac calumniis in Pezelium, Zanchium, Tossanum &c. insignis; Samuel Huberus, et Aegidius Hunnius, irrequieta ingenia, novis, etiam de Praedestinatione, feturis turgida: Cumprimis vero Flaccius Illyricus cum suis, iniquissimus insectator Philippi, ac emendatae ab eo Confessionis Augustanae, licet ipso cohortante Luthero, a quo Flacciani, et Flaccio-Brentiani, furoribus notissimi: Tandem Auctores Libri Concordiae, seu Formulae Bergensis, primipilis Jac. Andreae, Selneccero, Chytreo, Chemnitio, &c. De cujus Auctoribus, Scriptione, Scopo, Articulis, Reprobatione, Approbatione, Apologia, Sequelis, &c. fuse Hospinianus, in Opere Concordia Discors, et Palatini in Admonitione Neostad.; Henr. Altingius, in Historia MS. Reformat. Palatinae, &c.

Ex istis facile constabit, esse hujusmodi Schisma inter Evangelicos natum, cui occasionem initio praebuit aemulatio Lutherum inter et Carolostadium, mox Lutherum inter et Zwinglium, pares hos eruditione, ac reformandi studio, in uno forte praesentiae Eucharisticae modo, discordes. Hinc genuit primo infelix Schisma, levius in suis primordiis de S. Coena dissidium; levius dico, vel ex Colloquio Marpurgensi, in quo silentium Lutherus addixerat, tum ex collatione Articuli x. Confessionis Augustanae, cum addita Phil. Melanchthonis deinceps Elucidatione, atque in hac praetermissa improbatione secus docentium. Sed fovit mox animorum sententiarumque divortium, ὀξυχολία quorundam et vehementia, ut fuere hominum ingenia, non postremis hoc ordine Jac. Andreae, vero Smidlino seu fabro contentionum; Tilem. Heshusio, fortunam Superintendentis Generalis totius Palatinatus, anno aetatis XXXII. ferre nescio; dein notis Joh. Marbachio, Fl. Illyrico, &c. Parturivit mox Ubiquitatis dogma, quod assertum quidem primo occasione Controv. Eucharisticae, sed tacitum postea Luthero ac missum omnino, ut et in Augustana Confess. Recruduit autem post Lutheri fata, propinatur Brentio, sed interpolaturis ac promoturis J. Andreae, Flaccianis, Bergensibus, &c. Unde illorum divortium ab Augustana Confessione qualem recognoverat et emendarat Melanchthon, cumprimis ad Artic. x. et discrimen per eos natum inter Confess. variatam et invariatam. Accesserunt odia, furor, vis, exacerbatio hinc inde.
english: Such were Johann Brenz, father of the Ubiquitarians; Jakob Andreae, from the carpenter's craft called Schmidlin, who would add much to the Brentians; Tilemann Heshusius, fire and flame of so many tumults; Johann Marbach, marked by new portents and calumnies against Pezel, Zanchi, Tossanus, and others; Samuel Huber and Aegidius Hunnius, restless tempers, swollen with new births even concerning Predestination: and above all Flacius Illyricus with his party, the most unjust persecutor of Philip and of the Augsburg Confession as Melanchthon had emended it — though Luther himself had encouraged that work — from whom the Flaccians, and the Flaccio-Brentians, are most noted for their furies: and at last the Authors of the Book of Concord, or Bergen Formula, with Jakob Andreae, Selnecker, Chytraeus, Chemnitz, and others as chief captains. Concerning its Authors, Writing, Scope, Articles, Reprobation, Approbation, Apology, Sequels, and so on, Hospinian treats at length in his work Concordia Discors, and the Palatines in the Neustadt Admonition; also Heinrich Alting in his manuscript History of the Palatine Reformation, and others.

From these things it will easily be plain that a Schism of this kind was born among Evangelicals, to which rivalry between Luther and Carolostadius first gave occasion, and soon rivalry between Luther and Zwingli — men equal in learning and in zeal for reform, yet discordant in one point, the mode of Eucharistic presence. Hence first arose the unhappy Schism, a dissent about the Holy Supper lighter in its beginnings; lighter, I say, both from the Marburg Colloquy, in which Luther had enjoined silence, and from comparing Article X of the Augsburg Confession with the Elucidation Melanchthon afterward added, in which the disapproval of those who teach otherwise was omitted. But soon the sharp anger (ὀξυχολία) and vehemence of certain men fostered the divorce of minds and opinions — such as men's tempers were — and not last in that order Jakob Andreae, truly a Schmidlin or smith of contentions; Tilemann Heshusius, who somehow could not bear the fortune of General Superintendent of the whole Palatinate at the age of thirty-two; then the notorious Johann Marbach, Flacius Illyricus, and others. Soon the dogma of Ubiquity was brought to birth — asserted indeed at first on the occasion of the Eucharistic Controversy, but afterward left silent by Luther and dropped altogether, as also in the Augsburg Confession. Yet it broke out again after Luther's death, poured out by Brenz, but interpolated and promoted by Jakob Andreae, the Flaccians, the Bergen men, and others. Hence came their divorce from the Augsburg Confession as Melanchthon had reviewed and emended it, especially at Article X, and the distinction they produced between the Confession as varied and as unvaried. Hatreds, fury, force, and exacerbation followed on every side.

source_text: per Germaniam; adeo ut etiam in optimos pientissimosque Principes insurgerent, qualiter in Fridericum III. Palatinum atrox tempestas excitata, incentoribus praecipue J. Andreae, Heshusio, Bidenbachio, ut scilicet Fridericum Pium Pace Religionis, & Societate Augustanae Confess. excluderent, frustra futuri in Comitiis Augustanis A. 1566. Absolvit ultimo Formula Concordiae primo Torgensis, Bergensis postea, de qua modo dictum, re vera Discordiae Formula, & duraturi Schismatis Complementum; reclamaturis statim, Ludovico Elect. Palatino, Lutheranis quanquam addictissimo, aliisque Principibus, sed & Theologis gravissimis, ut fuse laudati Hospinianus, Altingius, &c. Sed diduxit ulcus in majus ac insanabile reddidit infelix Controversia de Praedestinatione, & annexis Capitibus nata praecipue, per Sam. Huberum, tum per Aegid. Hunnium Wittenbergensem, circa A. 1580. vel teste infra Georgio Calixto ad Confessionem Thorunensem, p. 14. Ac tandem obfirmarunt in hunc usque diem Evangelicor. istud dissidium, Satanae κακοτεχνία; occultae Jesuitarum artes τῶν πολυμηχάνων; Politicorum rationes Romae servientium, aut commodis suis; ac Theologorum plerumque κακοζηλία, typhus, odia, calumniae, praejudicia, scripta eristica & virulenta, ac privata in plurimis studia, ut accidit, nec habitura finem, donec Serenissimorum Principum auctoritate, ac vi majore, si interveniat unquam, coerceantur.
english: through Germany — so far that they rose even against the best and most pious Princes: as when a fierce tempest was stirred against Frederick III of the Palatinate, with Jakob Andreae, Heshusius, and Bidenbach as chief firebrands, that they might shut pious Frederick out of the Peace of Religion and the Society of the Augsburg Confession — though they would fail at the Augsburg Diet of 1566. At last the Formula of Concord finished the work — first the Torgau Formula, afterward the Bergen — of which we have just spoken: in truth a Formula of Discord, and the complement of a lasting Schism. Elector Ludwig of the Palatinate protested at once, though most devoted to the Lutherans, and other Princes with him, and also the weightiest Theologians — Hospinian, Alting, and the rest already praised at length. But the unhappy Controversy concerning Predestination and its annexed Heads, born chiefly through Samuel Huber and then through Aegidius Hunnius of Wittenberg around the year 1580 — or so Georg Calixtus testifies below on the Confession of Thorn, p. 14 — drew the ulcer wider and rendered it incurable.

And at last they have hardened that Evangelical dissent down to this very day: Satan's malign craft (κακοτεχνία); the hidden arts of the many-scheming Jesuits (τῶν πολυμηχάνων); the calculations of Politicians who serve Rome or their own advantage; and among Theologians for the most part a spiteful rivalry (κακοζηλία), pride, hatreds, calumnies, prejudices, eristic and virulent writings, and private ambitions in very many cases — as it happens — and it will have no end until, by the authority of the Most Serene Princes and by a greater force if one ever intervenes, they are coerced.

source_text: Caeterum in materia Tolerantiae mutuae, fraternaeque Concordiae, quaesitae inter Protestantium Ecclesias, non confundenda est (ut vellent) Lutheranorum, qui sic vocantur causa, cum illa hodiernorum Remonstrantium, de quorum Schismate non par Reformatis judicium fuit, & quorum Dogmata prolixe ante recensita. Minus conferenda Augustanorum Fratrum causa, in negotio Irenico, cum Pontificiorum altera, componant licet utramque Methodistae hodierni Romanenses. Unde nos utrique, & Remonstrantes & Pontificii, pridem ad Syncretismum in Religione sollicitarunt, intuitu oblatae communionis fratribus Confessionis Augustanae. Ac fecerunt Pontificii quidem, in ea Methodo quam Richelianam vocant, & quam revocavit nuper Clerus Gallicanus, in Methodo 1. inducendis nobis per Missionarios suos ad Communionem cum Rom. Ecclesia; In specie quoque urfit idem Condomiensis, nunc Meldensis Episcopus, Expositionis Catholicae seu Tridentinae, Cap. II.
english: But in the matter of mutual Tolerance and of fraternal Concord sought among the Churches of Protestants, the cause of those called Lutherans must not be confused — as some would wish — with that of today's Remonstrants, concerning whose Schism the Reformed judgment was not the same, and whose Dogmas were reviewed at length above. Still less is the cause of the Augsburg Brethren, in the irenic business, to be set beside that of the Pontiffs, though today's Roman Methodists may try to compose both. Hence both parties — Remonstrants and Pontiffs alike — have long solicited us toward Syncretism in Religion, with an eye to the communion offered to the brethren of the Augsburg Confession. And the Pontiffs have done so in that Method they call Richelian, which the Gallican Clergy lately revived, as Method 1: leading us by their Missionaries into Communion with the Roman Church. In particular the same Bishop of Condom, now of Meaux, pressed it in Chapter II of his Catholic or Tridentine Exposition.

source_text: Obtentus est, 1. Lutheranos defendere Praesentiam realem (ut vocant) Corporis Christi in Eucharistia; unde sequatur, quam tantopere refugimus, praesentis in Eucharistia Corporis adoratio. 2. Defendere eosdem dogma Ubiquitatis, ex quo sequatur omnino, Humanitatis Christi destructio: Et tamen paratos esse Reformatos illis communionem suam offerre, quia hoc destructae Humanitatis Consectarium negant; quidni & Pontificiis, Consequentias quae ex Doctrina Tridentina inferuntur, pariter refpuentibus? Sed huic vanissimae Methodo fuse, & ex professo, ivimus obviam in Stricturis nostris adversus Condomiensem tum Episcopum; editis A. 1681. Ubi nos pluribus, 1. De ratione tolerantiae & communionis qualis Fratribus Augustanae Confessionis oblata est; retorsione facta in Pontificios, tolerantiae imo humanitatis nescios, dum tamen dissensum a Rom. Ecclesia esse Fundamentalem negant. 2. Ibidem nos de dogmate Ubiquitatis, quatenus censetur convellere, aut non convellere fundamentum; facta collatione cum dogmatibus Pontificiorum controversis, eorumque praxi, longe alia ratione Christianismi essentiam perimentibus. 3. Ibi & nos de Praesentia reali ex mente Lutheranorum, & adoratione qualem probant in Eucharistia; enarrato longa serie discrimine, a dogmate Transubstantiationis, & Sacrificii Missatici, & Latriae Hostiae exhibitae, etiam extra usum Sacramenti; Praeter actus alios Idololatricos, & impense superstitiosos, in Missaticis Pontificiorum Sacris. 4. Tandem de Consequentis, quas causatur Meldensis Episcopus Reformatos non sine calumniae labe elicere ex doctrina Tridentina, pluribus nos in praefatis Stricturis.
english: The pretense was, first, that the Lutherans defend the so-called real Presence of Christ's Body in the Eucharist, from which would follow the Adoration of the Body present in the Eucharist — which we so greatly flee. Second, that they defend the dogma of Ubiquity, from which would follow altogether the destruction of Christ's Humanity: and yet the Reformed are ready to offer them their communion, because they deny that consequence of a destroyed Humanity — why then not also to Pontiffs who equally refuse the Consequences drawn from Tridentine Doctrine? But we went openly and at length against this vainest Method in our Strictures against the then Bishop of Condom, published in 1681.

There we treat at length: (1) of the reason of tolerance and of the communion offered to the brethren of the Augsburg Confession — with a retort upon Pontiffs who know nothing of tolerance, indeed of humanity, while they still deny that dissent from the Roman Church is Fundamental; (2) of the dogma of Ubiquity, how far it is held to overthrow the foundation or not — compared with the contested dogmas of the Pontiffs and with their practice, which destroy the essence of Christianity by a far other reason; (3) of real Presence in the Lutheran sense, and of the adoration they approve in the Eucharist — narrating in a long series the difference from the dogma of Transubstantiation, from the Mass Sacrifice, and from Latria of the Host shown even outside the use of the Sacrament, besides other idolatrous and intensely superstitious acts in the Pontiffs' Mass rites; (4) finally of the Consequences which the Bishop of Meaux charges the Reformed with eliciting from Tridentine doctrine not without the stain of calumny — treated by us at length in those Strictures.

source_text: Nec par sane ratio est causae Remonstranticae & Lutheranae, etiam in negotio Praedestinationis, annexorumve Capitum. Docent vel superiora, ubi suam suorumque mentem Rintelenfes Theologi explicuerunt, defensam ab iisdem postea in Apologia sua. Et appellamus in hac causa Lipsiacos, Gerhardum, Calixtum, imo Calovium in Considerat. Arminianismi, &c. sed ante omnia Lutherum ipsum. Nec enim ulla de Praedestinatione, vel de totali Impotentia servi Arbitrii, vel de Providentia Dei circa actiones malas, cum Luthero controversia fuit, doctrinam Augustini, quae & Pauli, fortiter asserente Libro de Servo Arbitrio, quem emisit contra Erasmum sub finem A. 1525. Nam in eo etiam occurrere horridiora de Decretis Divinis, & de peccandi necessitate, quam in Calvino ipso, fassi omnes ingenui, quaecunque effugia Lutheri nepotes captave-
english: Nor indeed is the Remonstrant cause and the Lutheran on equal footing, even in the business of Predestination and its annexed Heads. The points above already teach as much, where the Rinteln Theologians explained their own mind and their party's, afterward defended by them in their Apology. And in this cause we appeal to the Leipzig men, to Gerhard, to Calixtus, even to Calov in his Consideration of Arminianism, and others — but before all to Luther himself. For there was no controversy with Luther concerning Predestination, or the total Impotence of the bound Will, or God's Providence about evil actions: he strongly asserted Augustine's doctrine — which is also Paul's — in the Book on the Bondage of the Will, issued against Erasmus toward the end of 1525. For in it there occur even more dreadful things concerning the Divine Decrees and the necessity of sinning than in Calvin himself — as all candid men confess, whatever escapes Luther's grandsons may have tried to seize.

source_text: rint. Ac confirmavit postea Lutherus, luculenta Praefat. in Epist. ad Romanos, & scriptis aliis, etiam Germanicis. Nulla etiam hoc de argumento Controversia Reformatis mota, vel in Formula Torgensi, seu Libro Concordiae A. 1577. vel in Colloquio Montis-Belligartensi, vulgato A. 1587. Quin notati in Formula Concordiae Synergistae; nempe qui statuerent συνεργίαν quandam Lib. Arbitrii, & Causas Conversionis esse Spiritum S. Verbum, & Voluntatem Hominis, qui imputatus error fuit Melanchthoni. Sic exorta inter Joh. Marbachium & Hieron. Zanchium contentione, Argentinae A. 1562. & hujus doctrina acerbissime exagitata, nulla gravis expostulatio fuit in argumento de Praedestinat. In qua doctrina judicarunt Arbitri, quos inter Schmidlinus, Tubinga evocatus, non magnam diversitatem esse. Nec ante Aegid. Hunnium Wittenbergae tum docentem, A. 1580. & Georg. Mylium Jenensem, diversam sententiam a recepta illa Augustini, (cui adhaesissent Invariatae Augustanae Confess. Theologi) in Ecclesias Scholasque reductam, monuit ipse Calixtus, Animadvers. ad Confess. Thorunens.
english: And afterward Luther confirmed it in a lucid Preface to the Epistle to the Romans and in other writings, even German ones. Nor was any Controversy on this argument moved against the Reformed — neither in the Torgau Formula or Book of Concord of 1577, nor in the Montbeliard Colloquy published in 1587. On the contrary, Synergists were marked in the Formula of Concord: namely those who set a certain synergy (συνεργία) of Free Will, and held the Causes of Conversion to be the Holy Spirit, the Word, and Man's Will — which error was imputed to Melanchthon. So when contention arose at Strasbourg in 1562 between Johann Marbach and Jerome Zanchi, and Zanchi's doctrine was most bitterly harassed, there was no serious remonstrance on the Predestination argument. In that doctrine the Arbiters — among them Schmidlin summoned from Tubingen — judged there was no great diversity.

Nor, Calixtus himself warns in his Animadversions on the Thorn Confession, was a sentence different from that received Augustinian view — to which the Theologians of the Unaltered Augsburg Confession had clung — brought back into Churches and Schools before Aegidius Hunnius, then teaching at Wittenberg in 1580, and Georg Mylius of Jena.

source_text: Igitur etiamnum hodie fatentur Theologi qui a Luthero denominantur, 1. Eligi certas personas ab aeterno, non propter praevisam fidem, sed eligi in fide, seu per fidem in Christum. 2. Electionis nullam esse causam impulsivam in nobis, sed totum salutis negotium a Deo suspendi. 3. Praevideri fidem in quibusdam, sed ut ex gratia Spiritus S. ut donum Dei, quoad ejus initium, progressum, perseverantiam. 4. Mortuos nos esse in peccatis, nec ullas esse residuas vires in homine lapso ad bonum spirituale, ad actus supernaturales Conversionis. 5. Gratiam Dei re vera praevenire omnem operationem hominis, nec in hoc ullas esse vires ad Conversionem, nisi a Gratia praeventas, excitatas, & motas; ut ad primam Gratiae acceptionem, se non habeant nisi passive, quod diserte Calixtus. 6. Non dari illam nisi ex decreto, de danda Gratia efficaci ad credendum; nec Deum quicquam praevidere, nisi dependenter a se ut causa prima, minus praevidere bonum spirituale in nobis. 7. Fidem esse fiduciam divinae gratiae, seu remissionis peccatorum, per & propter Christum, contradistinctam jam operibus, in negotio Justificationis; darique salutis subjectivam certitudinem. 8. Electionem certarum Personarum esse aeternam, & immutabilem, adeoque Electos κατὰ πρόγνωσιν finaliter excidere non posse, ex hypothesi divinae Praescientiae, quae sit infallibilis. 9. Quoad Reprobationem, quanquam haud aliam velint, quam secundum praescientiam finalis Impoenitentiae, tamen non negant hoc modo aeternam eam esse; Aeternam adeo discretionem esse electorum a reprobis, hujus discretionis comparativae causam, esse Dei beneplacitum; Praescientiam etiam reproborum esse infallibilem. 10. Denique omnem se damnare Pelagianismum, Semi-Pelagianismum. Ut a scopo & mente Remonstrantium longe abfuisse appareant genuini Lutheri nepotes.
english: Therefore even now today the Theologians named from Luther confess: (1) that certain persons are elected from eternity, not because of foreseen faith, but elected in faith, or through faith in Christ; (2) that Election has no impulsive cause in us, but the whole business of salvation hangs upon God; (3) that faith is foreseen in some, yet as from the grace of the Holy Spirit, as God's gift, as to its beginning, progress, and perseverance; (4) that we are dead in sins, and that there are no residual powers in fallen man toward spiritual good, toward the supernatural acts of Conversion; (5) that God's Grace truly precedes every operation of man, and that in him there are no powers toward Conversion except those prevented, excited, and moved by Grace — so that toward the first reception of Grace they have themselves only passively, as Calixtus expressly says;

(6) that that grace is not given except from a decree of giving efficacious Grace for believing; nor does God foresee anything except dependently on Himself as first cause, still less foresee spiritual good in us; (7) that Faith is trust in divine grace, or in the remission of sins, through and on account of Christ, already contradistinguished from works in the business of Justification; and that a subjective certainty of salvation is given; (8) that the Election of certain Persons is eternal and immutable, and so the Elect according to foreknowledge (κατὰ πρόγνωσιν) cannot finally fall away, on the hypothesis of divine Foreknowledge, which is infallible; (9) as to Reprobation, although they want no other than according to foresight of final Impenitence, yet they do not deny that in this way it is eternal — that the distinction of elect from reprobate is eternal, that the cause of this comparative distinction is God's good pleasure, and that Foreknowledge of the reprobate also is infallible; (10) finally that they condemn every Pelagianism and Semi-Pelagianism. So genuine grandsons of Luther appear to have stood far from the aim and mind of the Remonstrants.
